title: Peripheral intravenous catheter failure before and after a change to clinically indicated replacement
subtitle: Cohort from existing flowsheet and surveillance data, adult medical and surgical wards
statement: On 1 March 2025 the hospital replaced routine resiting of peripheral intravenous catheters every 96 hours with replacement only when clinically indicated. Ward nurses disagree about whether longer dwell has brought more phlebitis and infiltration, and the nursing executive is concerned about bloodstream infections. A cohort comparing catheters inserted in the 12 months before and after the change will estimate whether catheter failure increased, and by how much insertions per admission fell.
whoAffected: Adults on the medical and surgical wards who need peripheral intravenous therapy, the ward nurses who insert and assess catheters, and the nursing executive and infection prevention team who own the policy.
whatHurts: A failed catheter interrupts treatment and means another painful insertion; a policy that raised failure would harm patients, while a return to routine resiting would bring back unnecessary insertions if the concern is unfounded.
currentPractice: Catheters stay in place while functioning and clinically needed, with a phlebitis score documented every shift; the removal reason is recorded in the vascular access flowsheet.
whyNow: Twelve months of data after the change now exist, the nursing executive wants an answer by June 2027, and ethics approval for secondary use is in place.
constraints: Secondary use of existing flowsheet and surveillance data only; no new data collection from patients. The clinical informatics team can give about 30 hours for data extraction. The nursing executive wants results by June 2027.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients receive intravenous treatment with as few insertions as possible and without more catheter failure or infection.
summary: Problem framed as a before-after cohort of catheters from existing records, with catheter failure as the main outcome.
